title: REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL
oneLiner: Three ways to shape the same API, compared on round trips, bytes on the wire and who carries the complexity.
keyTakeaway: REST is the default for public APIs: every language and tool speaks it, and HTTP caching works for free. gRPC is the usual choice between internal services: a typed contract in a .proto file, generated clients, compact binary messages over HTTP/2 and streaming in both directions, at the cost of browser support and human-readable traffic. GraphQL lets each client ask for exactly the fields it needs in one round trip, which suits apps with many different screens, but moves the cost to the server (N+1 queries, expensive queries, harder caching). Many companies use all three: GraphQL or a backend for frontend at the edge, gRPC inside, REST for partners.
explanation:
The same functionality can be exposed in several API styles, and interviewers like to ask why you picked one. The three you need to know are REST, gRPC and GraphQL; webhooks and streaming connections fill gaps none of them cover.

REST, covered in the previous lesson, maps resources to URLs and actions to HTTP methods, usually with JSON bodies. Its strengths are reach and simplicity: anything that can make an HTTP request can call it, you can try it with curl, and the web's caching layers (browsers, CDNs, reverse proxies) understand GET and Cache-Control without any extra work. OpenAPI (formerly Swagger) describes a REST API in a YAML or JSON file from which documentation and client libraries are generated. The weaknesses show up when a client needs data from several resources: a profile screen might call /users/7, then /users/7/posts, then /posts/{id}/comments for each post. That is several round trips, which is painful on a mobile network where each one costs 100 ms or more, and each response carries every field of the resource whether the screen uses it or not (overfetching). Teams fix this with query parameters that select fields or embed related resources (?fields=name,avatar&include=posts), or with a backend for frontend (BFF): a thin server per client type that makes the many calls inside the datacenter and returns one shaped response.

RPC (remote procedure call) is the older idea of making a call to another machine look like a local function call: GetUser(id) rather than GET /users/{id}. gRPC is Google's open-source RPC framework and the common choice between internal services. You write the contract in a .proto file using Protocol Buffers: messages with numbered, typed fields and services with methods. A compiler generates client and server code for each language, so a renamed field or a wrong type is a build error rather than a production incident. Messages are encoded in a compact binary format (field numbers and values, no field names), typically several times smaller and faster to parse than the same JSON. gRPC runs on HTTP/2, which multiplexes many calls over one long-lived connection, and it supports four call shapes: unary (one request, one response), server streaming, client streaming and bidirectional streaming. Deadlines travel with each call. The costs: browsers can't speak native gRPC (gRPC-Web and a proxy are needed), binary traffic is harder to inspect and debug, HTTP caches don't understand it, and long-lived HTTP/2 connections need load balancing per request rather than per connection (an L7 proxy such as Envoy), or one backend gets all the traffic.

GraphQL, released by Facebook in 2015, exposes a single endpoint and a typed schema of objects and the relations between them. The client sends a query naming exactly the fields it wants, nested as deep as the screen needs: the user's name and avatar, their last three posts, and each post's comment count, in one request whose response has the same shape as the query. That removes both the round trips and the overfetching, and lets mobile and web teams build new screens without waiting for a new endpoint. Writes are mutations, and subscriptions push updates. The cost moves to the server. Each field is filled by a resolver function, and a naive resolver for "comment count of each post" runs one database query per post: the N+1 query problem. The standard fix is a DataLoader, which collects the ids requested in one tick and fetches them in one batched query. A client can also write a query that is very expensive (deeply nested friends of friends), so servers limit query depth and assign each query a cost, and many only accept persisted queries (pre-registered query ids) from their own apps. Because every request is a POST to one URL, CDN caching and per-endpoint metrics and rate limits need extra work.

Two more tools complete the picture. A webhook reverses the direction: instead of a client polling "has the payment settled yet?", the provider sends an HTTP POST to a URL the client registered when something happens. Webhooks must be signed (an HMAC of the body with a shared secret, so the receiver can verify the sender) and are delivered at least once, so the receiver deduplicates by event id. For pushing a live stream to a browser, use server-sent events (SSE, one-way over plain HTTP) or WebSockets (two-way); long polling is the fallback when neither is available.

How to choose in an interview: say who the clients are. Unknown third-party developers, many languages, cacheable reads: REST. Internal services you control, high call volume, low latency, streaming: gRPC. Your own apps, many screens with different data needs, a team willing to run the server-side machinery: GraphQL, or a REST BFF. Then name what you give up. The widget fetches the same profile screen in each style, so you can see the round trips and bytes change, and then asks you to pick a style for six situations.
